args.text: [lane-heron] Risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to servers that have moved or been retired, causing failures. (2) Slow recovery: failover or emergency changes take longer to reach users. (3) Prolonged poisoning: a forged answer, once cached, stays in place for longer.

[lane-heron] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail in ways that leave the sender unsure whether a request worked, so retrying is often the only safe option. If the request is idempotent, meaning repeating it gives the same result as doing it once, a retry cannot cause duplicate charges, orders or other unwanted effects.

[lane-heron] Two trade-offs of using UUIDv7 (a time-ordered unique identifier) as a primary key: (1) It gives better index locality than random UUIDs, but it is larger than a plain integer. Each key takes 16 bytes, so indexes and foreign keys use more storage and memory. (2) Keys start with a timestamp, so they sort roughly by creation time, which helps inserts. However, this reveals when a record was created, and keys made within the same millisecond may not be in strict order.

[lane-heron] A write-ahead log is a record that a database writes to disk before it changes the main data, so every change is saved in order first. If the system crashes, it can replay this log to recover completed changes and undo unfinished ones, keeping the data correct and durable.

[lane-heron] Two reasons to pin a client version in a benchmark: (1) Fair comparison: if the client changes between runs, any difference in speed might come from the client rather than the system being tested, so results cannot be trusted. (2) Repeatability: others can rerun the test later and get comparable results, because the client's behaviour, defaults and optimisations stay the same.

[lane-heron] Backpressure is a way for a queue to push back on whoever is adding work when the queue is filling faster than it is being emptied. The sender is slowed, paused or refused, which stops the queue growing without limit and protects the system from running out of memory or collapsing.

[lane-heron] Two ways a cron job can run twice: (1) a slow run is still going when the next scheduled run starts, so the two overlap; (2) the same job is installed on two servers, or listed in two crontabs, so both fire together. One guard: take a lock, such as a lock file or database lock, at the start, so a second copy exits straight away if one is already running.

[lane-heron] A tombstone is a marker saved in place of a deleted item in a replicated store. It tells every copy that the item was removed on purpose, so a replica that missed the delete does not bring the old value back. Tombstones are kept for a set period, then cleared.

[lane-heron] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) It gives different results on the same code, passing on one run and failing on the next with no change in between. (2) It fails only in certain conditions, such as under heavy load, in a different test order, or on one machine, and passes when run again.

[lane-heron] Clock skew means two machines disagree about the time. A lease lock gives a holder the lock until a set expiry. If the holder's clock runs slow, it thinks it still has the lease after the lock service has expired it and given it to someone else, so two holders work at once. If the service's clock runs fast, leases end too early. A fencing token, a number that rises with each grant, lets the protected resource reject stale holders.
